<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite growing enthusiasm for Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), where multiple LLM agents collaborate to accomplish tasks, their performance gains across popular benchmarks remain minimal compared to single-agent frameworks.
This gap highlights the need to analyze the challenges hindering MAS effectiveness.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we present the first comprehensive study of MAS challenges. We analyze five popular MAS frameworks across over 150 tasks, involving six expert human annotators.
We identify 14 unique failure modes and propose a comprehensive taxonomy applicable to various MAS frameworks. This taxonomy emerges iteratively from agreements among three expert annotators per study, achieving a Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.88. These fine-grained failure modes are organized into 3 categories: (i) specification and system design failures, (ii) inter-agent misalignment, and (iii) task verification and termination.
To support scalable evaluation, we integrate MASFT with LLM-as-a-Judge. We also explore if identified failures could be easily prevented by proposing two interventions: improved specification of agent roles and enhanced orchestration strategies. Our findings reveal that identified failures require more complex solutions, highlighting a clear roadmap for future research.
We open-source our dataset and LLM annotator
<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        https://github.com/multi-agent-systems-failure-taxonomy/MASFT</span></span></span>.</p>
  
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, Large Language Model (LLM) based agentic systems have gained significant attention in the AI community <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patil et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Packer et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
This growing interest comes from the ability of agentic systems to handle complex, multi-step tasks while dynamically interacting with diverse environments, making LLM-based agentic systems well-suited for real-world problems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Building on this characteristic, multi-agent systems are increasingly explored in various domains, such as software engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024d</a>)</cite>, drug discoveries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gottweis et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Swanson et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, scientific simulations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023b</a>)</cite>, and recently general-purpose agent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2503.13657v1/multi_agent_systems_failure_rates_ucb.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/251;" width="452" height="251"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Failure rates of five popular Multi-Agent LLM Systems with GPT-4o and Claude-3.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although the formal definition of agents remains a topic of debate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cheng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, in this study, we define a LLM-based <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">agent</span> as an artificial entity with prompt specifications (initial state), conversation trace (state), and ability to interact with the environments such as tool usage (action).
A <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">multi-agent system</span> (<span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MAS</span>) is then defined as a collection of agents designed to interact through orchestration, enabling collective intelligence.
MASs are structured to coordinate efforts, enabling task decomposition, performance parallelization, context isolation, specialized model ensembling, and diverse reasoning discussions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mandi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2503.13657v1/taxonomy_v11_cropped.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:467/238;" width="467" height="238"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>A <span id="S1.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Taxonomy of MAS Failure Modes</span>. The inter-agent conversation stages indicate when a failure can occur in the end-to-end MAS system. If a failure mode spans multiple stages, it means the issue involves or can occur at different stages. Percentages represent how frequently each failure mode and category appeared in our analysis of 151 traces. Detailed definition and example of each failure mode is available in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A MASFT Failure Categories: Deep Dive ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite increasing adoption of MAS, the gain in accuracy or performance remains minimal compared to single agent frameworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xia et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or even simple baselines such as best-of-N sampling on popular benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Our empirical analysis reveals that the correctness of the state-of-the-art (SOTA) open-source MAS, ChatDev <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, can be as low as 25%, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Furthermore, there is no clear consensus on how to build robust and reliable MASs.
This leads to a fundamental question that we need to answer first: Why do MASs fail?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To understand MAS failure modes, we conduct the first systematic evaluation of MAS execution traces using Grounded Theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glaser &amp; Strauss, 1967</a>)</cite>.
We analyze five popular open-source MASs, employing six expert annotators to identify fine-grained issues across 150 conversation traces, each averaging over 15,000 lines of text.
We define failures as cases where the MAS does not achieve the intended task objectives.
To ensure consistency in failure modes and definitions, three expert annotators independently label 15 traces, achieving an inter-annotator agreement with a Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.88.
From this comprehensive analysis, we identify 14 distinct failure modes, which we cluster into 3 primary failure categories.
We introduce the <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">M</span>ulti-<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">A</span>gent <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">S</span>ystem <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">F</span>ailure <span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">T</span>axonomy (<span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>), the first structured failure taxonomy of MAS, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We do not claim MASFT covers every potential failure pattern; rather, it serves as the first step towards taxonomizing and understanding MAS failures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To enable scalable automated evaluation, we introduce an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> that uses OpenAI’s o1. To validate this pipeline, we cross-verify its annotations against three human expert annotations on 10 traces, obtaining a final Cohen’s Kappa agreement rate of 0.77.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, better specifications <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stoica et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> and prompting strategies could potentially mitigate MAS failures.
To test this hypothesis, we implement best-effort interventions using prompt engineering and enhanced agent topological orchestration.
Our case study with AG2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> and ChatDev <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2023</a>)</cite> reveals that although these interventions yield a +14% improvement for ChatDev, they do not resolve all failure cases.
Moreover, the improved performance remains insufficiently low for real-world deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">These findings suggest that <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> is not merely an artifact of existing multi-agent frameworks, but rather indicative of fundamental design flaws in MAS.
Towards building robust and reliable MAS, <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> serves as a framework for guiding future research, outlining potential solutions for each of the 14 failure modes. Additionally, we open source our annotations for further research in MAS.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">While one could simply attribute these failures to limitations of present-day LLM (e.g., hallucinations, misalignment), we conjecture that improvements in the base model capabilities will be insufficient to address the full <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>.
Instead, we argue that good MAS design requires organizational understanding – even organizations of sophisticated individuals can fail catastrophically <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perrow, 1984</a>)</cite> if the organization structure is flawed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Previous research in high-reliability organizations has shown that well-defined design principles can prevent such failures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roberts, 1989</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rochlin, 1996</a>)</cite>.
Consistent with these theories, our findings indicate that many MAS failures arise from the challenges in inter-agent interactions rather than the limitations of individual agents.
<span id="S1.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> enables systematic identification of these failures and informs the the design principles for next-generation MAS.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The contributions of this paper are as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p11" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>, the first empirically grounded <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">taxonomy of MAS failures</span>, providing a structured framework for understanding and mitigating MAS failures.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop a scalable LLM-as-a-judge <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">evaluation pipeline</span> for analyzing new MAS performance and diagnosing failure modes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct best-effort <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">interventions studies</span> targeting agent specification, conversation management, and verification strategies. Despite achieving an improvement of 14% on task completion, they fail to fully address MAS failures, highlighting the need for structural MAS redesigns.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We fully <span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">open-source</span>: (1) all 150+ annotated MAS conversation traces, (2) the scalable LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipeline and the LLM annotation on 150+ traces, and (3) detailed expert annotations on 15 selected traces.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Challenges in Agentic Systems</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The promising capabilities of agentic system has inspired research into specific agentic challenges. For instance, Agent Workflow Memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024e</a>)</cite> addresses long-horizon web navigation by introducing workflow memory.
DSPy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khattab et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Agora <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024e</a>)</cite> tackle issues in communication flow, and StateFlow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> focuses on state control within agentic workflows to improve task-solving capabilities.
While these works meaningfully contribute towards particular use cases, they do not provide a comprehensive understanding of why MASs fail or propose a strategy that can be broadly applied across domains.
Numerous benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate agentic systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jimenez et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anne et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bettini et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Long et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
These evaluations are crucial in identifying challenges and limitations in agentic systems, yet they primarily facilitate a top-down perspective, focusing on higher-level objectives such as task performance, trustworthiness, security, and privacy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Design Principle for Agentic Systems</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several works highlight the challenges of building robust agentic systems and suggest new strategies, typically for single-agent designs, to improve reliability.
For instance, Anthropic’s blog post <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024a</a>)</cite> draws the importance of modular components, such as prompt chaining and routing, rather than adopting overly complex frameworks. Similarly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapoor et al. (2024)</a></cite> shows that complexity can hinder real-world adoption for agentic systems.
Our work extends these insights by systematically investigating the failure modes in MASs, offering a taxonomy that demonstrates why MASs fail, and suggesting solutions that align with these insights for agentic system design.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Failures Taxonomization in LLM Systems</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the growing interest in LLM agents, dedicated research on their failure modes is surprisingly limited.
In parallel to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al. (2024)</a></cite>’ study that catalogs challenges in human-agent interaction in agentic system, our contribution represents a pioneering effort in studying failure modes in MASs.
This highlights the need for future research in developing robust evaluation metrics, identifying common failure patterns, and designing mitigation strategies to improve the reliability of MASs.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section describes our methodology for identifying dominant failure patterns in MAS and establishing a structured taxonomy of failure modes. Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> provides an overview of this workflow.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To systematically uncover failure patterns without bias, we adopt the <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Grounded Theory</span> (GT) approach <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glaser &amp; Strauss, 1967</a>)</cite>, a qualitative research method that constructs theories directly from empirical data rather than testing predefined hypotheses.
The inductive nature of GT allows the identification of the failure mode to emerge organically. We collect and analyze MAS execution traces iteratively with <em id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">theoretical sampling</em>, <em id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">open coding</em>, <em id="S3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">constant comparative analysis</em>, <em id="S3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">memoing</em>, and <em id="S3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">theorizing</em>, detailed in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Data Collection and Analysis ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">After obtaining the MAS traces and discussing our initial findings, we derive a preliminary taxonomy by gathering observed failure modes. To refine the taxonomy, we conduct inter-annotator agreement studies, iteratively adjusting the failure modes and the failure categories by adding, removing, merging, splitting, or modifying the definition until consensus is reached. This process mirrors a <em id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">learning</em> approach, where taxonomy refinement continues until achieving stability, measured by inter-annotator agreement through Cohen’s Kappa score. Additionally, to enable automated failure identification, we develop an LLM-based annotator and validate its reliability.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Data Collection and Analysis</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">theoretical sampling</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draucker et al., 2007</a>)</cite> to ensure diversity in the identified MASs, and the set of tasks on which to collect data (MAS execution traces).
This approach guided the selection of MASs based on variations in their objectives, organizational structures, implementation methodologies, and underlying agent personas. For each MAS, tasks were chosen to represent the intended capabilities of the system rather than artificially challenging scenarios. For example, if a system reported performance on specific benchmarks or datasets, we selected tasks directly from these benchmarks.
The analyzed MASs span multiple domains and contexts, as explained in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Multi-Agent Systems studied with human-annotated traces ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.
Upon collecting the MAS traces, we apply <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">open coding</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Khandkar, 2009</a>)</cite> to analyze the traces we collected for agent–agent and agent–environment interactions.
Open coding breaks qualitative data into labeled segments, allowing annotators to create new codes and document observations through memos, which enable iterative reflection and collaboration among annotators. In particular, the annotators identify the failure modes they encounter and systematically compare the new codes they created with the existing ones, also called as the <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">constant comparative analysis</span> in GT.
This iterative process of failure mode identification and open coding continues until we reached <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">theoretical saturation</span>, the point at which no new insights emerged from additional data. Through this process, the annotators annotated 150+ traces spanning 5 MASs. Next, we group related open codes to reveal the fine-grained failure modes in an initial version of <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>.
Finally, we link failure modes, forming a taxonomy of error categories as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. This process is denoted with points 1 and 2 in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Upon coming up with the initial taxonomy, one important question is how reliable this taxonomy is and how can we find an automated way of evaluating MAS failures given our taxonomy. To that end, we conduct internannotator agreement studies where three annotators aim to validate, refine and finalize the taxonomy that is derived here initially.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Interannotator Agreement Study and Iterative Refinement</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Inter-annotator studies mainly target validating a given test or rubric, such that when multiple different annotators annotate the same set of test cases based on the same rubric, they should arrive at the same conclusions. Even though we initially derive a taxonomy as a result of our theoretical sampling and open coding as explained in the previous section, there still exists the need to validate the non-ambiguity of this taxonomy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For inter-annotator agreements, we conduct three major rounds of discussions on top of the initial derivation of taxonomy. In Round 1, we sample 5 different MAS traces from over 150 traces we obtained with theoretical sampling as explained in the previous section, and the three annotators annotate these traces using the failure modes and definitions in the initial taxonomy. We observe that the agreement reached at Round 1 is very weak between annotators, with a Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.24. Next, these annotators work on the taxonomy to refine it. This involves iteratively changing the taxonomy until we converge to a consensus regarding whether each and every failure mode existed in a certain failure mode or not in all 5 of the collected traces. In iterative refinement, we change the definitions of failure modes, break them down into multiple fine grained failure modes, merge different failure modes into a new failure mode, add new failure modes or erase the failure modes from the taxonomy, as needed.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This process can be likened to a <em id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">learning</em> study where different agents (this time human annotators) independently collect observations from a shared state space and share their findings with each other to reach a consensus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lalitha et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. Moreover, in order not to fall into the fallacy of using training data as test data, when we do the refinement studies at the end of Round 1, we test the new inter-annotator agreement and the performance of the taxonomy in a different set of traces, in Round 2.
In the next stage (Round 2), we sample another set of 5 traces, each from a different MAS. Then, the annotators agred substantially well on the first try, attaining an average Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.92 among each other. Motivated by this, we proceed to Round 3, where we sampled another set of 5 traces and again annotated using the same finalized taxonomy, where achieved an average Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.84. Note that Cohen’s Kappa score of more than 0.8 is considered strong and more than 0.9 is considered almost perfect alignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">McHugh, 2012</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the reliability of our taxonomy, we ask the following question: can we come up with an automated way to annotate traces such that developers or users can use this automated pipeline with our taxonomy to understand the failure reasons of their models? Thus, we developed an automated <span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> annotator using an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline, which we describe in Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 LLM Annotator ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<span id="S3.T2.4.3.6.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:37.8pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.4.3.6.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.T2.4.3.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">0.77</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>LLM Annotator</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After developing our taxonomy, <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> and completing the inter-annotator agreement studies, we aim to come up with an automated way to discover and diagnoze the failure modes in MAS traces using our taxonomy. To that end, we develop an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline. In this strategy, we provide a system prompt to LLMs where we include the failure modes in our <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>, their detailed explanation, as shown in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A MASFT Failure Categories: Deep Dive ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, and some examples of these failure modes as shown in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Examples of Different Failure Modes ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
In that strategy, we decide to use OpenAI’s o1 model, and we experiment with both the cases where we do not provide the aforementioned examples (called o1 in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Interannotator Agreement Study and Iterative Refinement ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) and where we provide the examples (called o1 few-shot in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Interannotator Agreement Study and Iterative Refinement ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Based on the results of Round 3 of inter-annotator agreement study mentioned in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Interannotator Agreement Study and Iterative Refinement ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we test the success of the LLM annotator, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Interannotator Agreement Study and Iterative Refinement ‣ 3 Study Methodology ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. As we achieve an accuracy of 94% and a Cohen’s Kappa value of 77%, we deem that the LLM annotator, with in context examples provided, to be a reliable annotator. Motivated by this result, we let the LLM annotator annotate the rest of the traces in the 150+ trace corpora we gathered, the result of which are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 Study Findings ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and the final taxonomy with the distribution of failure modes is shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Study Findings</h2>

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2503.13657v1/masft_bar.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/153;" width="452" height="153"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Distribution of failure modes by categories and systems.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The Grounded Theory study and the inter-annotator agreement studies we performed on a diverse set of MASs resulted in the development of <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> presented in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
<span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> organizes 3 overarching failure categories, identifying 14 fine-grained failure modes that MASs can encounter during their execution.
<span id="S4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> also divides a MAS execution into 3 phases pertaining to agents: Pre-Execution, Execution and Post-Execution, identifying the MAS execution phases in which each of the fine-grained failure modes can occur.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Failure Categories</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we briefly describe the overarching failure categories (<span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FC</span>) in <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>.
Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A MASFT Failure Categories: Deep Dive ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> provides detailed definition for each of the 14 fine-grained failure modes in <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>.
Further, appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Examples of Different Failure Modes ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> provides detailed examples for each of the fine-grained failure modes in <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS1.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="98.4" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 98.4" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,98.4) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#0000BF;" fill="#0000BF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 92.5 C 0 95.76 2.64 98.4 5.91 98.4 L 471.47 98.4 C 474.73 98.4 477.38 95.76 477.38 92.5 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2FF;" fill="#F2F2FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 92.5 C 1.97 94.67 3.73 96.43 5.91 96.43 L 471.47 96.43 C 473.65 96.43 475.41 94.67 475.41 92.5 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.84 12.53)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.08em;--ltx-fo-height:5.49em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="78.72" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 76.03)" width="457.73"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.SS1.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:33.08em;">
<span id="S4.SS1.p2.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FC1. Specification and System Design Failures.<span id="S4.SS1.p2.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Failures arising from deficiencies in the design of the system architecture, poor conversation management, unclear task specifications or violation of constraints, and inadequate definition or adherence to the roles and responsibilities of the agents.</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In MAS, task failures often arise from incomplete or ambiguous instructions.
However, even when clear specifications are given, the MAS can be misaligned with user inputs.
An example of this category of failure is the violation of the task specification.
When asked to come up with a two-player chess game that takes as input classical chess move notation such as ’Ke8’,’Qd4’, the MAS framework ChatDev produces a game that takes as inputs <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x_{1},y_{1}),(x_{2},y_{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, which represent the initial coordinates of a piece on the chess board and the final coordinates of the piece, thus not satisfying the initial requirements.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Another failure mode of this category is the nonadherence of the role specification.
For instance, in ChatDev’s <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">DemandAnalysis</span> phase, the <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CPO</span> agent occasionally assumed the <span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CEO</span>’s role by unilaterally defining the product vision and making final decisions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS1.p5.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="79.11" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 79.11" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,79.11) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#0000BF;" fill="#0000BF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 73.2 C 0 76.46 2.64 79.11 5.91 79.11 L 471.47 79.11 C 474.73 79.11 477.38 76.46 477.38 73.2 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2FF;" fill="#F2F2FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 73.2 C 1.97 75.38 3.73 77.14 5.91 77.14 L 471.47 77.14 C 473.65 77.14 475.41 75.38 475.41 73.2 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.84 9.84)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.08em;--ltx-fo-height:4.29em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="59.42" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 59.42)" width="457.73"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.SS1.p5.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:33.08em;">
<span id="S4.SS1.p5.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FC2. Inter-Agent Misalignment.<span id="S4.SS1.p5.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Failures arising from ineffective communication, poor collaboration, conflicting behaviors among agents, and gradual derailment from the initial task.</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-agent systems often suffer from conversational inefficiencies, where agents engage in unproductive exchanges, consuming computational resources without meaningful progress.
For example, in a ChatDev trace involving the creation of a Wordle-like game, the <span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Programmer</span> agent interacted with multiple roles (<span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CTO</span>, <span id="S4.SS1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CCO</span>, etc.) across seven cycles but failed to update the initial code.
The resulting game was playable but lacked robustness, with only five simple words, undermining replayability and rendering additional communication rounds wasteful.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2503.13657v1/phone-agent-narrow.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/87;" width="429" height="87" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Phone Agent fails to communicate the API specifications and login username requirements to the Supervisor.
At the other end of the conversation, the Supervisor Agent also fails to seek clarification on the login details.
After a few back-and-forth attempts, the Supervisor Agent marks the task as failed.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">A different type of failure mode in this category is agents witholding valuable information.
For example, in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Failure Categories ‣ 4 Study Findings ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, a supervisor agent instructs a phone agent to retrieve contact information using an email ID as the username.
The phone agent, after reading the documentation and finding that the correct username should be a phone number, still proceeds with the wrong credentials, leading to an error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS1.p8.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="81.8" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 81.8" width="477.38"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,81.8) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#0000BF;" fill="#0000BF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 75.89 C 0 79.15 2.64 81.8 5.91 81.8 L 471.47 81.8 C 474.73 81.8 477.38 79.15 477.38 75.89 L 477.38 5.91 C 477.38 2.64 474.73 0 471.47 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2FF;" fill="#F2F2FF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 75.89 C 1.97 78.07 3.73 79.83 5.91 79.83 L 471.47 79.83 C 473.65 79.83 475.41 78.07 475.41 75.89 L 475.41 5.91 C 475.41 3.73 473.65 1.97 471.47 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 9.84 12.53)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:33.08em;--ltx-fo-height:4.29em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="62.11" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 59.42)" width="457.73"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.SS1.p8.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:33.08em;">
<span id="S4.SS1.p8.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p8.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">FC3. Task Verification and Termination.<span id="S4.SS1.p8.pic1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Failures resulting from premature execution termination, as well as insufficient mechanisms to guarantee the accuracy, completeness, and reliability of interactions, decisions, and outcomes.</span></span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">MASs may have been developed without a dedicated verification step, or they might include a verifier agent that fails to perform its task effectively.
For example, in a ChatDev scenario involving a chess game implementation, the verifier agent only checks if the code compiles without running the program or ensuring compliance with chess rules.
Chess is a well-established game with extensive specifications, rules, and implementations readily available online.
Even simple retrieval should intuitively prevent trivial failures, such as accepting malformed input.
However, without proper verification, defects like invalid input handling or malformed interfaces persist, rendering the game unplayable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Failure Analysis &amp; Implication</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 Study Findings ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows the distribution of the fine-grained failure modes along with the failure categories across the studied MASs.
Different colors represent the different failure categories in <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> and different shades represent the different fine-grained failure modes within a category.
We highlight that no single error category disproportionately dominates, demonstrating the diverse nature of failure occurrences and the robustness of the taxonomy used to classify them.
Furthermore, we note, as expected, that different MASs exhibit varying distributions of failure categories and modes.
For example, AG2 has fewer instances of inter-agent misalignment compared to specification and verification issues, whereas ChatDev encounters fewer verification issues than specification and inter-agent misalignment challenges.
These differences arise from the varying problem settings, which influence system topology design, communication protocols, and interaction management.
In turn, these factors shape systems with their own strengths and weaknesses.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 4.2 Failure Analysis &amp; Implication ‣ 4 Study Findings ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> highlights the correlation between different failure categories in <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>.
The correlations observed are not particularly strong, they indicate that the proposed taxonomy is a reasonable classification framework.
Moreover, this suggests also that failures are not isolated events; rather, they may have a cascading effect that can influence other failure categories.
For further details, see Figure <a href="#A3.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C MAS Failure Modes Correlation ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in the appendix that reports the correlation between different failure modes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2503.13657v1/masft_fc_corr.png" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:452/373;" width="452" height="373" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>MAS failure categories correlation matrix.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>It’s all your verifier’s fault?</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have identified a series of failure modes in MASs.
However, it can be argued that, at the end of the day, every failure could stem from a lack of proper verification or incorrect verification processes.
If we assume that the verifier agent functions perfectly, then all failures would be detectable and thus avoidable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In our study, we focus on verification issues in cases where the system can effectively benefit from the results of the verification process.
However, we also examine other failure modes that occur prior to the final verification step.
In many cases, we can consider verification as the last line of defense against failures.
This leads us to conclude that, while many issues may indeed be traced back to inadequate verification, not every problem can be solely attributed to this factor.
Other elements, such as poor specification, inadequate design, communication inefficiencies, also contribute to failures.
Therefore, a comprehensive approach to understanding and addressing failures in MASs must consider a broader range of factors beyond just verification shortcomings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span><span id="S4.SS4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> Failure Modes violate HRO Defining Characteristics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Even though we encountered some common LLM failure modes like text-repetition, we exclude them from <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> as these issues do not pertain specifically to MAS, and can occur even in single-LLM call pipelines.
On the other hand, we find evidence of MAS facing similar issues as complex human organizations, as the failure modes align with common failure modes observed in human organizations.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roberts &amp; Rousseau (1989)</a></cite> identifies eight primary characteristics shared by High-Reliability Organizations (HROs).
<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> discovered through GT, without any prior biases, includes several failure modalities that correlate with unique characteristics of HROs as identified by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roberts &amp; Rousseau (1989)</a></cite>.
Specifically, “<span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FM1.2</span>: Disobey role specification”</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where the agents try to overstep their roles, violates the HRO characteristic “Extreme hierarchical differentiation”.
Similarly, “<span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FM2.2</span>: Fail to ask for clarification” undermines “Deference to Expertise”.
The direct violation of HRO characteristics by the failure modes identified in <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span> serves as validation for the applicability of <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_bold">MASFT</span>, and the need for non-trivial interventions inspired by HRO.
For example, to prevent “<span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">FM1.2</span>: Disobey role specification” from occuring in MAS, the orchestration and persona assignment can enforce hierarchical differentiation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Towards better Multi-Agent LLM Systems</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we discuss some approaches to make MASs more robust to failures.
We categorize these strategies into two main groups:
(i) <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">tactical approaches</span>,
(ii) <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">structural strategies</span>.
Tactical approaches involve straightforward modifications tailored for specific failure modes, such as improving the prompts, topology of the network of agents, and conversation management.
In Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we experiment with such approaches in two case studies, and demonstrate that the effectiveness of these methods is not consistent.
This leads us to consider a second category of strategies that are more comprehensive methods with system-wide impacts:
strong verification, enhanced communication protocols, uncertainty quantification, and memory and state management.
These strategies require more in-depth study and meticulous implementation, and remain open research topics for future exploration. See Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Structural Strategies ‣ 5 Towards better Multi-Agent LLM Systems ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> for our proposed mapping between different solution strategies and the failure categories.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Tactical Approaches</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This category includes strategies related to improving prompts and optimizing agent organization and interactions.
The prompts of MAS agents should provide clear description of instructions, and the role of each agent should be clearly specified (see <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Structured prompt with verification section ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a> as an example) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Talebirad &amp; Nadiri, 2023</a>)</cite>.
Prompts can also clarify roles and tasks while encouraging proactive dialogue. Agents can re-engage or retry if inconsistencies arise, as shown in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Agent Verifier’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
After completing a complex multi-step task, add a self-verification step to the prompt to retrace the reasoning by restating solutions, checking conditions, and testing for errors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Weng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
However, it may miss flaws, rely on vague conditions, or be impractical <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stoica et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
Moreover, clear role specifications can be reinforced by defining conversation patterns and setting termination conditions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">LangChain, 2024</a>)</cite>.
A modular approach with simple, well-defined agents, rather than complex, multitasked ones, enhances performance and simplifies debugging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024b</a>)</cite>.
The group dynamics also enable other interesting possibilities of multi-agent systems: different agents can propose various solutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, discuss their assumptions, and findings (cross-verifications) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Haji et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
For instance, in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, a multi-agent strategy simulates the academic peer review process to catch deeper inconsistencies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Another set of tactical approaches for cross verifications consist in multiple LLM calls with majority voting or resampling until verification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stroebl et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.
However, these seemingly straightforward solutions often prove inconsistent, echoing our case studies’ findings. This underscores the need for more robust, structural strategies, as discussed in the following sections.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Structural Strategies</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Apart from the tactical approaches we discussed above, there exist a need for more involved solutions that will shape the structure of the MAS at hand.
We first observe the critical role of verification processes and verifier agents in multi-agent systems.
Our annotations reveal that weak or inadequate verification mechanisms were a significant contributor to system failures.
While unit test generation aids verification in software engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jain et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, creating a universal verification mechanism remains challenging. Even in coding, covering all edge cases is complex, even for experts. Verification varies by domain: coding requires thorough test coverage, QA demands certified data checks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and reasoning benefits from symbolic validation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kapanipathi et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Adapting verification across domains remains an ongoing research challenge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A complementary strategy to verification is establishing a standardized communication protocol <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
LLM-based agents mainly communicate via unstructured text, leading to ambiguities. Clearly defining intentions and parameters enhances alignment and enables formal coherence checks during and after interactions.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Niu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> introduce Multi-Agent Graph Attention, leveraging a graph attention mechanism to model agent interactions and enhance coordination. Similarly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang &amp; Lu, 2018</a>)</cite> propose Attentional Communication, enabling agents to selectively focus on relevant information. Likewise, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2018</a>)</cite> develop a learned selective communication protocol to improve cooperation efficiency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another important research direction is fine-tuning MAS agents with reinforcement learning.
Agents can be trained with role-specific algorithms, rewarding task-aligned actions and penalizing inefficiencies.
MAPPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> optimizes agents’ adherence to defined roles.
Similarly, SHPPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> uses a latent network to learn strategies before applying a heterogeneous decision layer.
Optima <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> further enhances communication efficiency and task effectiveness through iterative reinforcement learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On a different note, incorporating probabilistic confidence measures into agent interactions can significantly enhance decision-making and communication reliability.
Drawing inspiration from the framework proposed by Horvitz et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Horvitz, 1999</a>)</cite>, agents can be designed to take action only when their confidence exceeds a predefined threshold.
Conversely, when confidence is low, agents can pause to gather additional information.
Furthermore, the system could benefit from adaptive thresholding, where confidence thresholds are dynamically adjusted.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Although often seen as a single-agent property, memory and state management are crucial for multi-agent interactions, which can enhance context understanding and reduces ambiguity in communication.
However, most research focuses on single-agent systems. MemGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Packer et al., 2023</a>)</cite> introduces OS-inspired context management for an extended context window, while TapeAgents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chakraborty &amp; Purkayastha, 2023</a>)</cite> use a structured, replayable log (“tape”) to iteratively document and refine agent actions, facilitating dynamic task decomposition and continuous improvement.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Case Studies</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we present the two case studies where we apply some of the tactical approaches.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Case Study 1: AG2 - MathChat</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this case study, we use the MathChat scenario implementation in AG2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> as our baseline, where a Student agent collaborates with an Assistant agent capable of Python code execution to solve problems.
For benchmarking, we randomly select 200 exercises from the GSM-Plus dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, an augmented version of GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite> with various adversarial perturbations.
The first strategy is to improve the original prompt with a clear structure and a new section dedicated to the verification.
The detailed prompts are provided in Appendices <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Initial prompt ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a> and <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Structured prompt with verification section ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.
The second strategy refines the agent configuration into a more specialized system with three distinct roles:
a Problem Solver who solves the problem using a chain-of-thought approach without tools (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS3" title="E.3 Agent Problem Solver’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3</span></a>);
a Coder who writes and executes Python code to derive the final answer (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS4" title="E.4 Agent Coder’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.4</span></a>);
a Verifier who reviews the discussion and critically evaluate the solutions, either confirming the answer or prompting further debate (see Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Agent Verifier’s System Prompt ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a>).
In this setting, only the Verifier can terminate the conversation once a solution is found.
See Appendix <a href="#A5.SS6" title="E.6 AG2 - MathChat: an example of conversation with three specialized agents ‣ Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.6</span></a> for an example of conversation in this setting.
To assess the effectiveness of these strategies, we conduct benchmarking experiments across three configurations (baseline, improved prompt, and new topology) using two different LLMs (GPT-4 and GPT-4o).
We also perform six repetitions to evaluate the consistency of the results.
Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ 6 Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> summarizes the results.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The second column of Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ 6 Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> show that with GPT-4, the improved prompt with verification significantly outperforms the baseline. However, the new topology does not yield the same improvement. A Wilcoxon test returned a p-value of 0.4, indicating the small gain is not statistically significant. With GPT-4o (the third column of Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ 6 Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), the Wilcoxon test yields a p-value of 0.03 when comparing the baseline to both the improved prompt and the new topology, indicating statistically significant improvements.
These results suggest that refining prompts and defining clear agent roles can reduce failures.
However, these strategies are not universal, and their effectiveness varies based on factors such as the underlying LLM.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Case Study 2: ChatDev</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ChatDev <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2023</a>)</cite> simulates a multiagent software company where different agents have different role specifications, such as a CEO, a CTO, a software engineer and a reviewer, who try to collaboratively solve a software generation task.
In an attempt to address the challenges we observed frequently in the traces, we implement two different interventions.
Our first solution is refining role-specific prompts to enforce hierarchy and role adherence.
For instance, we observed cases where the CPO prematurely ended discussions with the CEO without fully addressing constraints.
To prevent this, we ensured that only superior agents can finalize conversations.
Additionally, we enhanced verifier role specifications to focus on task-specific edge cases.
Details of these interventions are in Section <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F ChatDev Prompt Interventions ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.
The second solution attempt involved a fundamental change to the framework’s topology.
We modified the framework’s topology from a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to a cyclic graph.
The process now terminates only when the CTO agent confirms that all reviews are properly satisfied, with a maximum iteration cutoff to prevent infinite loops.
This approach enables iterative refinement and more comprehensive quality assurance.
We test our interventions in two different benchmarks. The first one of them is a custom generated set of 32 different tasks (which we call as ProgramDev) where we ask the framework to generate programs ranging from “Write me a two-player chess game playable in the terminal” to ”Write me a BMI calculator”. The other benchmark is the HumanEval task of OpenAI. We report our results in Table <a href="#S6.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 6.2 Case Study 2: ChatDev ‣ 6 Case Studies ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Notice that even though our interventions are successful in improving the performance of the framework in different tasks, they do not constitute substantial improvements, and more comprehensive solutions as we lay out in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Structural Strategies ‣ 5 Towards better Multi-Agent LLM Systems ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a> are required.</p>
</div>

<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this study, we present the first systematic investigation of failure modes of LLM based Multi-Agent Systems, where we collect and analyze more than 150+ traces with the guidance of Grounded Theory, and iteratively refine our taxonomy and validate through an inter-annotator study.
We identify 14 fine-grained failure modes, and group them under 3 different failure categories, providing a rubric for future research in MASs.
We also propose an LLM Annotator as an automated way to analyze MAS traces, and show its validity and reliability.
We also discuss two sets of solutions for all the failure categories, tactical and structural strategies. Upon conducting case studies with some of the tactical strategies, our findings indicate that many of these “obvious” fixes actually possess severe limitations, and need the structural strategies we outlined for more consistent improvements.</p>
</div>

</section>
