<section id="Ax1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix">Organization of Appendix</h2>

<div id="Ax1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Ax1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The appendix is organized as follows:
in Section <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A MASFT Failure Categories: Deep Dive ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> further details about failure categories and failure modes are given,
in Section <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Multi-Agent Systems studied with human-annotated traces ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> we provide some details about the multi-agent systems we have annotated and studied,
in Section <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C MAS Failure Modes Correlation ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> we plot the correlations between MAS failure modes,
in Section <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Examples of Different Failure Modes ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> examples of every failure mode are reported and commented,
in Sections <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E AG2 - MathChat Scenario ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a> and <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F ChatDev Prompt Interventions ‣ Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> there are prompt interventions we tested on AG2 and ChatDev case studies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>MASFT Failure Categories: Deep Dive</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>FC1. Specification and System Design Failures</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This category includes failures that arise from deficiencies in the design of the system architecture, poor conversation management, unclear task specifications or violation of constraints, and inadequate definition or adherence to the roles and responsibilities of the agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We identify five failure modes under this category:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-1.1: <span id="A1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Disobey task specification</span> - Failure to adhere to the specified constraints or requirements of a given task, leading to suboptimal or incorrect outcomes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-1.2: <span id="A1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Disobey role specification</span> - Failure to adhere to the defined responsibilities and constraints of an assigned role, potentially leading to an agent behaving like another.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-1.3: <span id="A1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Step repetition</span> - Unnecessary reiteration of previously completed steps in a process, potentially causing delays or errors in task completion.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-1.4: <span id="A1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Loss of conversation history</span> - Unexpected context truncation, disregarding recent interaction history and reverting to an antecedent conversational state.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-1.5: <span id="A1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unaware of termination conditions</span> - Lack of recognition or understanding of the criteria that should trigger the termination of the agents’ interaction, potentially leading to unnecessary continuation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>FC2. Inter-Agent Misalignment</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This category includes failures arising from ineffective communication, poor collaboration, conflicting behaviors among agents, and gradual derailment from the initial task.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We identify six failure modes under this category:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-2.1: <span id="A1.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Conversation reset</span> - Unexpected or unwarranted restarting of a dialogue, potentially losing context and progress made in the interaction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-2.2: <span id="A1.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fail to ask for clarification</span> - Inability to request additional information when faced with unclear or incomplete data, potentially resulting in incorrect actions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-2.3: <span id="A1.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task derailment</span> - Deviation from the intended objective or focus of a given task, potentially resulting in irrelevant or unproductive actions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-2.4: <span id="A1.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Information withholding</span> - Failure to share or communicate important data or insights that an agent possess and could impact decision-making of other agents if shared.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-2.5: <span id="A1.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ignored other agent’s input</span> - Disregarding or failing to adequately consider input or recommendations provided by other agents in the system, potentially leading to suboptimal decisions or missed opportunities for collaboration.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I2.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I2.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-2.6: <span id="A1.I2.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reasoning-action mismatch</span> - Discrepancy between the logical reasoning process and the actual actions taken by the agent, potentially resulting in unexpected or undesired behaviors.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>FC3. Task Verification and Termination</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This category includes failures resulting from premature execution termination, as well as insufficient mechanisms to guarantee the accuracy, completeness, and reliability of interactions, decisions, and outcomes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We identify three failure modes under this category:</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="A1.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A1.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-3.1: <span id="A1.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Premature termination</span> - Ending a dialogue, interaction or task before all necessary information has been exchanged or objectives have been met, potentially resulting in incomplete or incorrect outcomes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-3.3: <span id="A1.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No or incomplete verification</span> - (partial) omission of proper checking or confirmation of task outcomes or system outputs, potentially allowing errors or inconsistencies to propagate undetected.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A1.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A1.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FM-3.3: <span id="A1.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Incorrect verification</span> - Failure to adequately validate or cross-check crucial information or decisions during the iterations, potentially leading to errors or vulnerabilities in the system.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Multi-Agent Systems studied with human-annotated traces</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide some more details on MAS we annotated during our study.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>MAS with at least 30 human annotated traces</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">MetaGPT.</span> MetaGPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is a multi-agent system that simulates a software engineering company and involves agents such as a Coder and a Verifier. The goal is to have agents with domain-expertise (achieved by encoding Standard Operating Procedures of different roles into agents prompts) collaborativelty solve a programming task, specified in natural language.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">ChatDev.</span>
ChatDev is a generalist multi-agent framework that initializes different agents, each assuming common roles in a software-development company <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The framework breaks down the process of software development into 3 phases: design, coding and testing. Each phase is divided into sub-tasks, for example, testing is divided into code review (static) and system testing (dynamic). In every sub-task, two agents collaborate where one of the agents acts as the orchestrator and initiates the interaction and the other acts as an assistant to help the orchestrator achieve the task. The 2 agents then hold a multi-turn conversation to achieve the goal stated by the orchestrator ultimately leading to the completion of the task, marked by a specific sentinel by either agents. ChatDev has the following agent roles: CEO, CTO, Programmer, Reviewer and Tester. ChatDev introduces “Communicative Dehallucination”, which encourages the assistant to seek further details about the task over multiple-turns, instead of responding immediately.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">HyperAgent.</span>
HyperAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> is a framework for software engineering tasks organized around four primary agents: Planner, Navigator, Code Editor, and Executor.
These agents are enhanced by specialized tools, designed to provide LLM-interpretable output.
The Planner communicates with child agents via a standardized message format with two fields: Context (background and rationale) and Request (actionable instructions).
Tasks are broken down into subtasks and published to specific queues.
Child agents, such as Navigator, Editor, and Executor instances, monitor these queues and process tasks asynchronously, enabling parallel execution and significantly improving scalability and efficiency.
For example, multiple Navigator instances can explore different parts of a large codebase in parallel, the Editor can apply changes across multiple files simultaneously, and the Executor can run tests concurrently, accelerating validation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">AppWorld.</span>
AppWorld is a benchmark, that provides an environment with elaborate mocks of various everyday services like eShopping Website, Music Player, Contacts, Cost-sharing app, e-mail, etc <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The benchmark consists of tasks that require executing APIs from multiple services to achieve the end-users tasks. The AppWorld benchmark provides a ReAct based agent over GPT-4o as a strong baseline. We create a multi-agent system over AppWorld derived from the baseline ReAct agent, where each agent specializes in using one of the services mocked in AppWorld, with detailed instructions about the APIs available in that service, and access to the documentation for that specific service. A supervisor agent receives the task instruction to be completed, and can hold one-on-one multi-turn conversations with each of the service-specific agents. The service-agents are instructed to seek clarification with the supervisor, whenever required. The supervisor agent holds access to various information about the human-user, for example, credentials to access various services, name, email-id and contact of the user, etc, which the service-agents need to access the services, and must clarify with the supervisor agent.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">AG2.</span> AG2 (formerly AutoGen) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is an open-source programming framework for building agents and managing their interactions.
With this framework, it is possible to build various flexible conversation patterns, integrating tools usage and customizing the termination strategy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>MAS with at least 5 human annotated traces</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">AutoKaggle.</span>
AutoKaggle is a multi-agent framework designed to solve data science competitions, popularly held on Kaggle, autonomously <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>. Similar to ChatDev above, AutoKaggle has a phase-based workflow. It divides the data science competition process into six key phases: background understanding, preliminary exploratory data analysis, data cleaning (DC), in-depth exploratory data analysis, feature engineering (FE), and model building, validation, and prediction (MBVP). AutoKaggle consists of 5 specialized agents: Reader, Planner, Developer, Reviewer and Summarizer. In each phase, a subset of these agents are active and work in sequence to complete the phase. The reader agent finds information relevant to the task, by reading the summary from the previous phase and makes observations about the current phase and includes them in an overview. The planner uses the overview to generate a plan to complete the current phase. Next, the developer agent uses tools like code execution, debugger and unit tests to write the code. AutoKaggle also provides a comprehensive set of machine learning tools, abstracting away complex code that would be required to perform compound data processing tasks like “FillMissingValues” into simple API calls that AutoKaggle agents can generate. The reviewer then provides feedback. Finally, the summarizer agent writes a detailed summary of the phase execution including changes (addition/deletions) to the data, and this summary is then passed to the next phase.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">Multi-Agent Peer Review.</span> Multi-Agent Peer Review <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is a collaboration strategy where each agent independently constructs its own solution, peer-reviews the solutions of others, and assigns confidence levels to its reviews.
Upon receiving peer reviews, agents revise their initial solutions, and the final prediction is determined through a majority vote among the n participating agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">MA-ToT.</span> Multi-Agent Tree of Thoughts leverage the strengths of both multi-agent reasoning and Tree of Thoughts (ToT) strategies. In this system, multiple Reasoner agents operate in parallel, employing ToT to explore diverse reasoning paths.
Then, a Thought Validator verifies these paths and promotes valid reasonings.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Example for FM-1.3 Step repetition, FM-2.1 Conversation reset, FM-1.2 Disobey role specification</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

<li id="A4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<p id="A4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MAS:</span> Hyperagent</p>

<li id="A4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
